# [The cost of decomposition in]{style="color: gray;"} risk-limiting election audits

## But what is an election audit? {style="--list-gap: 1.8em"}

- After an election, we get a reported outcome:
  * Who won
  * [Possibly: a digital record of each vote (CVRs)]{.fragment .strikeout fragment-index=1} [Ballot-polling]{.fragment .after-strike fragment-index=1 style="color: #d6195f;"}

- An *election audit* checks it against the ground-truth *audit trail*
  * (e.g. original paper ballots)
  * If the audit concludes it is correct $\longrightarrow$ *Certify!*
  * Otherwise, something went wrong $\longrightarrow$ *recount!*

::: notes
- Timing: 1 minute.
- when: after the election
  * after all votes have been submitted
  * and after they have all been counted
  * when reported outcome is available
- why:
  * check that it is correct---outcome may come from electronic systems with bugs
  * want to verify with high confidence without redoing the whole count by hand (expensive)
- (NEXT) I study ballot polling audits, that get minimal information and are easier
  * Only know who won
  * And have access to the ground-truth ballots
:::

## *Risk-limiting* audits {style="--list-gap: 1.5em"}

- Election audits are hypothesis tests

- Control Type I error probability at level $\alpha$ [(e.g. 0.05)]{.side}
  * If the reported outcome is wrong:  $\mathrm{P}[\text{recount}]\geq 1-\alpha$.

- If it is correct:
  * we want to confirm that using as few ballots as possible
  * Goal: minimise the *expected* sample size

::: notes
- A Risk-limiting audit (or RLA) frames the election audit as a statistical hypothesis test
- Specifically, we control Type~I error at some predetermined level alpha
- If in fact the reported outcome is wrong, we correct it with probability at least 1-alpha
- If it is correct, then the goal is to prove that
- By observing as few ballots (and thus as cheaply) as possible
- To do that, we may want minimise the average number of ballots required, for instance
:::


## The hypothesis test {style="--list-gap: 2em"}

- $H_0$: the reported outcome is incorrect
  * reject $H_0\longrightarrow$ certify

- $H_1$: The reported outcome is correct
  * accept $H_0\longrightarrow$ recount
  * recounts are expensive!! 
  * some audits never accept $H_0$: they are "power-one"


## Sequential test

- Observing votes sequentially: $X_1,X_2,\dots$

- Construct a stochastic process $E_t$
  * $E_t$ summarises the "evidence for $H_1$ against $H_0$"

<canvas class="evidence" data-stat="bf" data-true="0.45,0.35,0.2" data-t="100" data-seed="1" data-alpha="0.05"
        style="width:100%; aspect-ratio:1664/420;"></canvas>

<span class="fragment suprema-step"></span>


## Why sequential tests? {style="--list-gap: 1.2em"}

- Accepting $H_0$ is expensive [(full recount!)]{.side}

- A fixed-sample test needs a huge sample for enough power

- Sequential tests need fewer samples on average [(occasionally many more)]{.side}

- The average is what matters:
  * elections keep happening [(…hopefully)]{.side}
  * many contests [(e.g. different seats)]{.side}


# Setting

## Plurality elections, with-replacement {style="--list-gap: 1.5em"}

- Plurality
  * Voters select only one candidate
  * Whoever gets the most votes wins

- Sampling with replacement
  * Observations are i.i.d.
  * $X_t \overset{d}{=} X_{t'}$
  * Not used in practice $\not\Rightarrow$ impractical!

## $K$-candidate plurality

- $\theta = (\theta_1,\theta_2,\dots,\theta_K)$ are the proportions of votes for each candidate

- Candidate 1 is the reported winner

- $H_0$: candidate 1 did not really win
  * $\theta_1\leq\theta_i$ *for some* $i\neq1$

- $H_1$: candidate 1 did win
  * $\theta_1>\theta_i$ *for all* $i\neq1$


## Two candidates (the easy case)

- Observations are $X_t \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(\theta)$.
- $H_0: \theta_1 \le 1/2$ against $H_1: \theta_1 > 1/2$.
- Very well-studied:
  * BRAVO [@bravo2012]
  * ALPHA [@alpha_mart]

```{.tikz width="100%"}
\begin{tikzpicture}[x=12cm, y=1cm]
  % Null H0: theta <= 1/2, shaded as in the ternary diagrams
  \fill[nullfill] (0,0) rectangle (0.5,1.4);

  % Axis
  \draw[thick] (0,0) -- (1,0);
  \foreach \x/\l in {0/0, 1/1} \draw (\x,0.12) -- (\x,-0.12) node[below] {$\l$};
  \draw[line width=1.1pt] (0.5,0.2) -- (0.5,-0.2) node[below] {$1/2$ (tie)};
  \node[right] at (1.02,0) {$\theta_1$};

  % Region labels
  \node at (0.25,0.7) {$H_0$};
  \node at (0.75,0.7) {$H_1$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

## Three candidates: the plurality null

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- $H_1 = \{\theta_1 > \theta_2 \text{ and } \theta_1 > \theta_3\}$
- $H_0 = \{\theta_1 \le \theta_2\} \cup \{\theta_1 \le \theta_3\}$
- A union of two half-spaces, and not convex.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{.tikz width="100%"}

  \coordinate (M13) at (barycentric cs:T1=1,T3=1);      % midpoint of T1--T3 edge

  % Shade H1 region: candidate 1 is the plurality winner
  \fill[nullfill] (T2) -- (M12) -- (G) -- (M13) -- (T3) -- cycle;

  % Simplex outline
  \draw[thick] (T1) -- (T2) -- (T3) -- cycle;

  % Decision boundaries theta1=theta2 and theta1=theta3
  \draw[line width=1.1pt] (M12) -- (G);
  \draw[line width=1.1pt] (G)   -- (M13);

  % Region labels
  \node at (barycentric cs:T1=0.5,T2=0.25,T3=0.25) {$H_1$};

  % Boundary labels

  \node[font=\small] at (barycentric cs:T1=0.35,T2=0.15,T3=0.5) {$\theta_1=\theta_3$};

  % Vertex labels
  \node[above]       at (T1) {$\theta_1$};
  \node[below left]  at (T2) {$\theta_2$};
```

- SHANGRLA: [[@stark2020shangrla]]{.side}
  * Test $H_{02}: \theta_1 \le \theta_2$ and $H_{03}: \theta_1 \le \theta_3$ separately
- Certify when every pairwise null is rejected: [an intersection-union test [@Berger1982]]{.side}


## Why not just do one test? {.center}

- Testing one-dimensional hypotheses is easy to do well.

- But could doing a single test in the original null do better?

- In the classical setting:
  * *some* intersection-union tests can be improved on [[@Berger1989]]{.side}

- In our setting it is an open problem


## Bayesian tests

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}

[Bayes factors (BF) are classically interpreted as summarising evidence for/against competing models.]{.side}

- Place a prior $W_1$ on $H_1$ and $W_0$ on $H_0$
- The BF is the marginal likelihood ratio $B_t = p_{W_1}(X^t) / p_{W_0}(X^t)$
- Bayesian audits track $B_t$ over time [[@bayesian_audits; @Huang_2020]]{.side}
- Reject when $B_t>\kappa$, chosen a priori
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{.tikz width="100%"}
\usetikzlibrary{calc}
\definecolor{wone}{HTML}{0072B2}   % Okabe-Ito blue       -> W_1
\definecolor{wzero}{HTML}{D55E00}  % Okabe-Ito vermillion -> W_0

  \coordinate (T2) at (0,0);

  \coordinate (G)   at (barycentric cs:T1=1,T2=1,T3=1);
  \coordinate (M12) at (barycentric cs:T1=1,T2=1);
  \coordinate (M13) at (barycentric cs:T1=1,T3=1);

  % H0 shading (bottom region)
  \fill[nullfill8] (T2) -- (M12) -- (G) -- (M13) -- (T3) -- cycle;

  % W1 contours (prior under the alternative), clipped to H1
  \begin{scope}
    \clip (T1) -- (M12) -- (G) -- (M13) -- cycle;
    \input{contours_h1.tex}
  \end{scope}

  % W0 contours (prior under the null), clipped to H0
  \begin{scope}
    \clip (T2) -- (M12) -- (G) -- (M13) -- (T3) -- cycle;
    \input{contours_h0.tex}
  \end{scope}

  % Simplex outline + decision boundaries
  \draw[thick] (T1) -- (T2) -- (T3) -- cycle;
  \draw[line width=1.1pt] (M12) -- (G);
  \draw[line width=1.1pt] (G)   -- (M13);

  % Region + prior labels
  \node at (barycentric cs:T1=0.62,T2=0.19,T3=0.19) {$H_1$};
  \node[wone, fill=white, inner sep=2pt, font=\small, yshift=-6pt] at (barycentric cs:T1=0.5,T2=0.27,T3=0.23) {$W_1$};
  \node[fill=nullfill8, inner sep=2pt] at (barycentric cs:T1=0.12,T2=0.46,T3=0.42) {$H_0$};
  \node[wzero, fill=nullfill8, inner sep=2pt, font=\small] at (barycentric cs:T1=0.22,T2=0.46,T3=0.32) {$W_0$};

  % Vertex labels
  \node[above]       at (T1) {$\theta_1$};
  \node[below left]  at (T2) {$\theta_2$};
```

## But Type I error control matters, {style="--list-gap: 1.5em"}

and unfortunately, choosing $\kappa$ to control Type I error at level $\alpha$ is hard.

- We want to select $\kappa$ such that $$\mathrm{P}_\theta\big(B_t>\kappa\text{ for some }t\big)\leq\alpha\text{ for all }\theta\in H_0.$$
- Later we will see that for some choices of $W_1, W_0$ this is easy.
- For others it will be impossible.

# Bayesian audits (last year)

## Controlling Type I error via truncation {style="--list-gap: 1.5em"}

- Fix a maximum sample size $T$ [(aka truncation)]{.side}
- Then $\bar B = \sup_{t \le T} B_t$ is bounded
- Compute the threshold by Monte Carlo:
  * estimate the $(1-\alpha)$--quantile
  * under the "worst-case null"

[movie time...]{.side}


::: notes
Timing: 1 minute.
The worst case being the two-way tie will come back: in the K = 2 likelihood ratio the tie is the whole story.
:::

## My findings {style="--list-gap: 1.5em"}

- The "worst-case null" is always the two-way tie (50/50 split, rest zero)
  * Proven for a symmetric Dirichlet priors
  * Otherwise somewhere on the boundary for a wider class

- It compares quite similarly to the (recalibrated) state of the art
  * State of the art threshold can be ~halved with $T=10,000$

- ...but it requires truncation at $T$

## What's wrong with truncation? {style="--list-gap: 1em"}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column style="width: 60%;"}
- It permits optional stopping
  * We are allowed to "peek" at the data
  * stop early if we have strong evidence

- But not optional continuation
  * Threshold $\kappa=100$
  * $T=1000$
  * What if $B_{1000}=99$?
:::

# Safe, anytime-valid inference


## E-variables {style="--list-gap: 2em;"}

- A nonnegative random variable $E$ with $\mathbb{E}_{P_\theta}[E] \le 1$ for every $\theta\in H_0$
- By Markov: reject when $E \geq 1/\alpha$ [(a loose bound, but buys a lot of freedom)]{.side}
- Independent (or conditional) e-variables can be multiplied
- The result is another e-variable

## Betting interpretation [[@Shafer2021]]{.side}

- The null model represents what the house believes
  * The house will accept any bet we propose...
  * ...provided it has expected value $\leq1$

- If $H_0$ is wrong, we should be able to win some money

- So we design a payoff $E$
  * We expect $E$ to be large
  * while under $H_0$, it does not make money on average

## Betting interpretation continued {style="--list-gap: 2em;"}

- Our winnings represent our evidence accumulated against $H_0$

- If someone walks into a casino with \$1 and walks out a millionaire...
  * ...something fishy is going on

- Winnings can be reinvested to gather more evidence


## Test supermartingales {style="--list-gap: 2em"}

- A *test supermartingale* is a nonnegative stochastic process $(S_t)$:
  * $S_0 = 1$ [(start with \$1)]{.side}
  * $\mathbb{E}_{P_\theta}[S_t | X_1,\dots,X_{t-1}]\leq S_{t-1}$ [(house always expects us to lose money)]{.side}

- @ville: $P(\sup_t S_t \ge 1/\alpha) \le \alpha$
  * "time-uniform" Markov's inequality
  * no $T$ needed!


## Anytime-validity {style="--list-gap: 1em"}

- Stop whenever you like!
  * the stopped process $S_\tau$ is an e-variable
  * $\tau$ can be any stopping time: "my boss told me to stop"

- Continue whenever you like!
  * reinvest the winnings
  * products of e-variables (from successive batches) are e-variables

- Safe!


## An e-variable we all know {style="--list-gap: 1.5em;"}

- E-variables generalise likelihood ratios [[@vovk2021evalues]]{.side}

- The simple likelihood ratio $\frac{p_\mu(X)}{p_\nu(X)}$ is an e-variable for $H_0:\theta=\nu$:
$$
\mathbb{E}_{P_\nu}\left[\frac{p_\mu(X)}{p_\nu(X)}\right] = 1
$$
- ...but what about composite nulls like $H_0: \theta\leq 1/2$?


## BRAVO [[@bravo2012]]{.side}

- Set $\mu$ to be the reported winners share ($>1/2$)

- Set $\nu = 1/2$

- The e-variable at time $t$ is the product of Bernoulli likelihood ratios:
$$
E_t = \prod_{i=1}^t \left(\frac{\mu}{\nu}\right)^{X_i}\left(\frac{1-\mu}{1-\nu}\right)^{1-X_i}
$$

- $(E_t)$ is a test supermartingale for every $\theta\leq1/2$ [(pretty nifty!)]{.side}


## The expected likelihood ratio

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
$$E_t = \prod_{i=1}^t \left(\frac{\mu}{\nu}\right)^{X_i}\left(\frac{1-\mu}{1-\nu}\right)^{1-X_i},
\qquad
g(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_\theta[E].$$
:::

```{=html}
<div id="gw1"></div>
<script>GW.line({ fig: "gw1", mu: 0.7, nu: 0.5, n: 10, nLabel: "t", name: "widget1" });</script>
```

::: notes
The curve always crosses 1 at theta = nu.

Demo: drag the blue triangle (mu) and the vermillion circle (nu) along the axis. nu snaps to 1/2.

1. Start at nu = 1/2: the curve crosses 1 exactly at the tie, valid.
2. Drag nu to 0.4: the curve crosses 1 at 0.4, and the band (0.4, 0.5] goes above 1 (thick stroke).
3. Drag nu to 0.55: valid again, but g<1 for all of H0, so it is "not the best choice" in some sense.
4. There is a t slider too that controls sample size, not sure if I will use it.
:::

## Which $\nu$ is best? {style="--list-gap: 1.5em;"}

- Every $\nu \in [1/2, \mu)$ gives an e-variable

- Judge by *growth rate* [(Kelly betting)]{.side}
$$\mathbb{E}_\mu[\log E_1] = \mathrm{KL}(P_\mu \,\|\, P_\nu)$$

- Expected samples to reject $\approx \log(1/\alpha) / \mathrm{KL}$

- Best: $\nu = 1/2$, the point in $H_0$ closest to $\mu$

## The resolution: mixtures over the null

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="70%"}
- Let $Q$ be *any* distribution for the numerator
  * generalises the choice of $P_\mu$
  * e.g. a marginal distribution w/ prior $W_1$ on $H_1$
- @safetesting:
  * there exists a prior $W^*$ on $H_0$ such that:
  * writing $P^*=P_{W^*}$: $q(X) / p^*(X)$ is an e-variable
  * the only MLR e-variable with $Q$ in the numerator
  * $P^*$ is *essentially unique* [($W^*$ may not be)]{.side}
:::
::: {.column width="30%"}
::: {style="position: relative; top: 100px;"}

## Reverse Information Projection [(RIPr)]{.side}

$W^*$ minimises the divergence of $P^*$ from $Q$ among all priors $W$ on $H_0$:
$$\mathrm{KL}(Q\,\|\,P^*) = \inf_W\, \mathrm{KL}(Q\,\|\,P_W)$$

- $q(X)/p^*(X)$ is log-optimal under $Q$
  * Best growth $\implies$ maximises KL among e-variables?
  * earlier, $P_\nu=P_{1/2}$ was the RIPr of $P_\mu$ onto $H_0$
- Finding $W^*$ is a convex optimisation problem (KL convex)
  * Numerical methods should do well...?

## Approximating the RIPr


:::{style="margin-top: 100px;"}
Minimising $\mathrm{KL}(Q \,\|\, P_W)$ is maximising the expected log-likelihood
$$\mathbb{E}_Q\left[\log\, p_{W}(X)\right]$$
:::
- Like fitting a mixture model to $Q$...
  * ...but with components constrained to $H_0$

## The algorithms

- "Oracles": adding one atom at a time
  - Li--Barron [@LiBarron1999]
  - Frank--Wolfe [@FrankWolfe1956; @Jaggi2013]
    * Recently applied to this problem by [@TuynmanMathieu2026]
- Expectation--maximisation [@DempsterLairdRubin1977]
  * no new atoms added
  * move and reweight 
- I find a hybrid (FW + EM) approach works well

::: notes
Timing: 1 minute.
The oracle, which picks where the next atom goes, is a global non-convex search. That is where the difficulty lives.
:::

## Close is not enough {style="--list-gap: 2em"}

:::{style="margin-top: 100px;"}
If $g_W(\theta) > 1$ anywhere in the null, $q(X)/p_W(X)$ is **not an e-variable**.
:::

- $q(X)/p^*(X)$ is the **only** e-variable of ratio form
  * $\implies$ approximations do not yield e-variables


## Fix: {style="--list-gap: 1.5em"}

- Just divide by the worst case $G_W = \sup_{\theta} g_W(\theta)$

- $E_W = \frac{1}{G_W}\frac{dQ}{dP_W}$ is an e-variable
- We get a free bound on the optimal growth:
$$\mathrm{KL}(Q\,\|\,P_W) - \log G_W \le \mathbb{E}_Q[\log E^*] \le \mathrm{KL}(Q\,\|\,P_W)$$
- An interval with width $\log G_W$!

::: notes
Timing: 1 minute. This is the central idea of the manuscript; slow down here.
Careful wording: exceeding 1 somewhere means invalid, not merely suboptimal.
:::

## Rigorous bounds for $G_W$

- Finding $G_W = \sup_{\theta} g_W(\theta)$ is a hard problem
  * Optimising may not find the global max
- We need a rigorous, global upper bound $U_W\geq G_W$
- Branch-and-bound algorithms:
  * divide $H_0$ into small regions
  * bound $g_W$ over the smaller pieces
  * smaller piece $\implies$ smaller bound
 
## Multinomial branch-and-bound

- $g_W(\theta)$ is a polynomial in $\theta$
  * "Bernstein polynomials"
  * Coefficients are the realisations of $q(X)/p_W(X)$

- Bernstein branch-and-bound [@Leroy2012]
  * global minimisation for polynomials

## BNB in action

# The ALE manuscript

<!-- Section budget: 3 minutes, 3 slides. -->

## ALE: testing under the influence with approximately log-optimal e-variables

With David and Damjan. arXiv target: November 2026.

1. A recipe that turns any approximate projection into an e-variable, with its growth bracketed.
2. A comparison of Li–Barron, Frank–Wolfe, EM and a new hybrid, on growth against wall-clock time.
3. Rigorous branch-and-bound bounds on $G_W$: Bernstein enclosures for multinomials, and a finiteness criterion for Gaussian location nulls.

- Open-source R package ripr.

## Question 1: how many atoms does the RIPr need?

- For $K = 3$ and a point alternative, two atoms suffice in every case I have run.
- Conjecture: $K - 1$ atoms suffice for a point alternative. Is there an analytic form?
- For mixture alternatives, almost certainly not.

## Question 2: how optimal are the pairwise martingales?

- At a fixed sample size nothing beats $E^*$, so the pairwise minimum is no better.
- $E^*$ is not a martingale, but batches of it multiply into one (optional continuation).
- How does the batch-sequential test compare with ALPHA per pair?
- Conjecture: batches win at moderate $n$, and the gap vanishes as $n \to \infty$, which would make the pairwise approach admissible.

::: notes
Timing: 1.5 minutes.
This is the question the thesis was organised around. It is the main study for November and December.
Expect the question: what happens if an audit has to stop mid-batch?

::: notes
Timing: 45 seconds.
The figure shows each pair as a projection to a one-dimensional problem with the tie as its null point.
:::


## It is a minimum {visibility="uncounted"}

- Certifying when every pair has rejected means thresholding $\min_j E_j$.
- $\min_j E_j$ is an e-variable for $\Theta_0 = \bigcup_j \Theta_{0j}$: under $\Theta_{0j}$ it is at most $E_j$.
- The log-optimal e-variable is a likelihood ratio $dQ/dP^*$.
- **Surely the optimum does not contain a min?**


## Why sampling with replacement? {visibility="uncounted"}

- A mathematical device, not a physical requirement: reuse ballots already drawn whenever the model asks for a repeat.
- The cost is the finite-population correction, expected to be small for large elections.

::: {.fetch}
slides/fig/alpha_sampling_effort.svg (recipe A).
:::


## Is any Bayes factor an e-process for $K > 2$? {visibility="uncounted"}

- For $K = 2$ the projection is the tie at every $n$, so the Bayes factor is a test martingale.
- For $K > 2$ preliminary calculations show the projection depends on $n$.
- Conjecture: no Bayes factor of this form is an e-process. Not yet proved.


## How does this differ from @TuynmanMathieu2026? {visibility="uncounted"}

- They fit the projection with Frank–Wolfe and stop when iterates stop changing
- No guarantees
- I accept the final iterate is as suboptimal
  * Restore validity via rigorous bounds
  * measure the gap and growth attained
  * Compute an interval that contains the log-optimal growth
- My Gaussian example goes beyond finite distributions
